title: Machine Learning Hamiltonians are Accurate Energy-Force Predictors
claim: The method is a staged flow from input through equivariant modules to a predicted object, from which final quantities are computed.
layout: 2 stacked panels: top overview flow, bottom detailed architecture, left-to-right
description: Two stacked panels, read left to right. Panel (a) is a row of rounded boxes joined by dark arrows: Input, Input Embedding, SO(2) Backbone, Two-stage Pair Update, Tensor Expansion, a predicted Hamiltonian H-hat, and a final E, F output. A small gray 'DFT Eval.' label sits on the last arrow. Panel (b) zooms into the architecture. On the left, H_t goes into a Matrix Encoder, which is concatenated with time t and molecular structure M. The result feeds a repeated stack of Edgewise Conv, Add & Norm, Nodewise Conv and Add & Norm blocks, marked ×L. A second block follows with Edgewise Conv, Tensor Product and Add & Norm. Node and edge feature circles carry math notation. Shades of blue distinguish SO(2)-equivariant from SO(3)-equivariant modules, explained in a legend at lower right. Skip connections loop above and below the blocks.
caption: QHFlow2 overall workflow. Given the molecular structure M, flow time t, and an intermediate Hamiltonian state Ht, QHFlow2 applies an SO(2) backbone, a two-stage pairwise update, and construct Hamiltonian via tensor expansion for energy and force evaluation. (a) Pipeline overview. (b) Detailed architecture of the matrix encode, the SO(2) backbone, and the two-stage pair update.
abstract: Recently, machine learning Hamiltonian (MLH) models have gained traction as fast approximations of electronic structures such as orbitals and electron densities, while also enabling direct evaluation of energies and forces from their predictions. However, despite their physical grounding, existing Hamiltonian models are evaluated mainly by reconstruction metrics, leaving it unclear how well they perform as energy-force predictors. We address this gap with a benchmark that computes energies and forces directly from predicted Hamiltonians. Within this framework, we propose QHFlow2, a state-of-the-art Hamiltonian model with an SO(2)-equivariant backbone and a two-stage edge update. QHFlow2 achieves $40\%$ lower Hamiltonian error than the previous best model with fewer parameters. Under direct evaluation on MD17/rMD17, it is the first Hamiltonian model to reach NequIP-level force accuracy while achieving up to $20\times$ lower energy MAE. On QH9, QHFlow2 reduces energy error by up to $20\times$ compared to MACE. Finally, we demonstrate that QHFlow2 exhibits consistent scaling behavior with respect to model capacity and data, and that improvements in Hamiltonian accuracy effectively translate into more accurate energy and force computations.
